items.body:
One of Coil’s most fêted longform works makes its maiden vinyl trip, all 50 minutes of wormhole ooze, now smeared over two sides of wax.

Up there with Coil’s ‘Time Machines’ or NWW’s ’Soliloquy For Lilith’ in the post-industrial canon, and echoing the sanguine psychedelic scope of La Monte Young & Marian Zalzeela’s zoned-out ‘70s staple as The Theatre of Eternal Music, there are very potent reasons why ‘Queens Of The Circulating Library’ is hailed among Coil’s finest. 

Introduced by opera singer Dorothy Lewis, who also happens to be Thingpaulsandra’s mother, it glacially shears off into Indian raga-like drones with a proper hypnagogic traction that’s likely soundtracked thousands of minds on the cusp of semi-consciousness during the years since its release on CD in 2000. With 2nd hand copies now pretty pricey, and YouTube compression only allowing for less-than-optimal potency, this edition is primed to take psychonauts where the piece was intended.

One of few Coil works without Sleazy at the desk, it features music by Thighpaulsandra and lyrics recited by his mum, especially written for “her and mothers everywhere” by John Balance, which perfectly teases minds into its amniotic suspension. Attentive pursuit may produce dreamlike effects, subtly generating fractal peripherals while the lustrous core absorbs deep into its whorls. It’s the sort of piece that warrants looping endlessly or until it takes ultimate effect and you’re bezonked on the deck/sofa/bed. A great way to while away winter.

items.body:
Oh man this is just incredible; Oren Ambarchi cracks open the work of lesser-known guitar god (and notorious instrument builder) Hans Reichel, selecting solo recordings spanning 1973-1988 that highlight his innovative approach to the instrument. It honestly sounds like nothing else, but followers of work by Oren Ambarchi, Fred Frith, Henry Kaiser, Derek Bailey or Keith Rowe - this will do you in.

Best known these days as the location of Open Ground, the German club opened by Mark Ernestus with one of the world's best soundsystems, North Rhine-Westphalia's Wuppertal is also the hometown of Hans Reichel, an improv titan and "experimental luthier" who genuinely changed the way improvisers approached the guitar. Don't take our word for it, guitarist (and Black Truffle boss) Oren Ambarchi credits Reichel with shaping his philosophy, and now celebrates the pioneer with a groegously compiled anthology of 23 tracks from his vast (and fairly impenetrable) catalog. Many might be familiar with Reichel mostly for his inventions, particularly the daxophone, an experimental idiophone he created to mimic animal sounds that's become a Hollywood staple in recent years, but the fact that his own work hasn't been raked over makes 'Dalbergia Refusa' a vital missing link, shining a spotlight on his work as both a player, composer and luthier - and it is quite honestly one of the most crucial reissues we’ve heard in years.

Ambarchi first came in contact with Reichel's work when he heard 1987's 'Return of the Knödler show' on a Guitar Player magazine cover disc -  and it soon changed the way Ambarchi thought about the instrument, you can very clearly hear its impact on his early recordings - especially his milestone 'Grapes From The Estate'. So it's a fitting way for Ambarchi to open the compilation - particularly because keen-eared listeners might recognise it for another reason, it's the track that Daniel Lopatin samples (and croons over) on 'No Good', 'Garden of Delete's light-headed highlight. With that one out of the way, the rest of the tracks really display Reichel's range: his technical skills using extra strings, moveable pickups or extra bridges, and his compositional boldness, freely shifting from solo guitar to multiple instruments or from pick to hammer.

'Wenn Das Rohr Dommelt', the opening track from Reichel's first album, 1973's 'Wichlinghauser Blues', foregrounded one of the artist's oddest instruments - an 11-string zither-style device that used piano strings and was hammered, with a shot glass used as a slide. It's shockingly unique sound that established a benchmark for Reichel as he went on to pull from US and UK rock and folk he grew up with, like on 'The call (I)' from 1979's ace 'The Death of the Rate Bird Ymir' - you can hear those ideas chewed up through his unique methodology. The American primitive concepts that Fahey distributed to a network of his acolytes sound different here, trampled by Reichel and his "full fret guitar" but not lost entirely. Similarly, there's an echo of psychedelic rock on the closing track 'Heimkehr der Holzböcke', taken from a rare 7" released in 1975, that Reichel corrodes with his advanced techniques, overdubbing bird-like squeaks and dissonant, blues-y plods. 

Another utterly indispensable history lesson from Black Truffle, then.

Really feeling this trippy acid treat by a one-of-a-kind Lolina; her 10th solo album since the last Hype Williams drop with Dean Blunt in the early 2010s, and typically riddled with low-key mischievous slants on mutant dance-pop, as heard in her regular midweek club night at ace London venue, Spanners.

Chasing up her trip-hop tinted LP ‘Unrecognisable’ (2024), and a mix CD as Balmainjeans repping her club night ‘Distressed’, Lolina plays to an ideally unpredictable form with a shift into acid pop on ‘Monopoly of Mistakes’; featuring eleven concentrated formulations of dry drum machines x tweakiest 303 gunk gilded with those vocals that keep us coming back. The combo of silver box x slanted vox finds the DIY prism-pusher bending timelines thru lo-fi indie-pop with sound system steppas, basement noise, cold wave and free party acid tekno, but never quite settling into any one style.

Maintaining her mutable range of variations within a theme, Monopoly of Mistakes really catches our breath with the way Lolina turns a paucity of ingredients into a dead satisfying thing. Whether commanding the 303 to the beat-less abstraction ‘Border Beach’ or alloying with wooziest keys and steppas fizz on ‘The Mercenaries’, or going deep into the lushest wormhole on the titular, 7 minute standout, her min-to-max sense of economy is key to this LP’s appeal. It’s there in the piquant synth-pop of ‘Menace’ and ‘Everlasting’ - think Wee Papa Girl Rappers via Dave Ball at John T. Gast’s - and calling to mind a lost SOPHIE x EVOL gem in ’Stand Off’. But it’s also finely measured with an utterly gorgeous new age miniature harking to classic Hype Williams on ‘Welcome to the Drift of Whats Already Begun’, and of course the zinging closer ‘Penalty’, where zippiest ‘80s french cold wave meets AFXian harmony and a sort of Dopplereffektish science-lab engineering in a chef’s kiss demo of the extended melodic wooo that sets all her work apart.

Best believe it’s fully distinctive, addictive gear.

items.body:
Peak Oil mooch in our back yard again with a strong album from YOUTH & Shotta Tapes alum Leo - the latest in their line of UK mutants (Paperclip Minimiser, Low End Activist, Wrecked Lightship) and a definitive statement of classic uk dub-as-method in electroid 2-step and crooked dembow forms.

A whirring cog in the Manchester machine, Leo has spent the 2020s rent in brooding negative space. His 4th album, ‘Cicada Burnt’ emerges in six segments that harness his drummer’s sleight of hand and feel for textured production on structures that teem with hi-tech sound design, insectoid detail and weathered pressure systems. No doubt it’s his most impressive artistic statement thus far, straddling key, extramusical reference points nabbed from his roots in Pennine Oldham landscapes and work strafing the industrial city downhill, and in that sense comparable with the Skam/NMB nexus or DDS’ cloud-seeding rufige.

Under the ochre artwork of Sean Clarke, who does Leo’s live visuals, the album smoulders with a dusky light and particulates in the air, conjuring immersive environmental settings and subtle tensions between the anticipatory rhythms and dread gloom. We can hear coruscating echoes of Paperclip Minimiser’s pendulous metric intricacy via Autechre in ‘Qwershape’, and his adroit percussive instincts on the tight electro-rolls of a ‘Jetti’ reminding us of Gescom's Cybotron-sampling classic 'Puzl', as well as low key Skam legend Mike Williamson - the guy behind that sick Grace Jones edit on Mask 400. His feel for syncopated nuance is zipped tightest in the grimy dembow of ‘Descant’, and likewise a weightless ‘Spirit Level (Prescript)’ demonstrating patiently poised, heightened proprioceptions, held in balance with the tendon-twitching steppas closer ‘Spirit Level’.

2023 Reissue of the very first Buddha Machine, newly upgraded with better sound quality and user experience including a louder speaker and 2 new individual side buttons to make the device control more direct and intuitive. Available in 5 colours.

You either know what these are and have already hit the buy button, or you’re too young to remember the Brian Eno-fuelled craze for these ambient boxes and are about to enter a portal to a different time. We must have sold several - many - thousands of these in their various iterations, including editions made in collab with Philip Glass and Throbbing Gristle, and after about a decade in the wilderness, they’re now back, in a new replica version of the very first edition from 2005 - that’s before the Iphone era - with improved controls and sound quality. oh, and that all important line out, for your buddha boxing!

In 2005 the Beijing-based duo of Christiaan Virant and Zhang Jian released their first, soon to be iconic  “Buddha Machine” loop box, a quirky pocket soundsystem that propelled sound art into the consumer mainstream. It spawned a whole cultural movement, fuelled by Brian Eno professing his love for them, and an era of live show "Buddha Boxing" improvisations.

The original version has been long sold-out and fetches crazy prices second hand, followed by various further iterations made in collaboration with Philip Glass and Throbbing Gristle. This new edition is a replica of the very fiest version, featuring the original loops in all their 8-bit Lo-Fi glory and available in 5 different colours.

"The classic loops of the original FM3 Buddha Machine evoke instant nostalgia for a slower, more simple world. Born before the iPhone era, this iconic device has weathered two decades of pop culture and fashion trends, yet remains defiantly, heroically unique. Its enduring simplicity cloaks an extraordinary power: the ability to transcend time. It is both a sonic portal to a hands-on analogue past and a bridge to a digital ever-present. This is not just a re-issue; it is a revival and refinement of a sonic manifesto that unfolds softly, gently and organically, resonating with the subtle rhythms of life. The Buddha 1 2023 edition from FM3. Available in 5 colours: Red, Orange, Green, Blue and limited-edition Pink. Features upgraded sound quality and user experience. Louder speaker and 2 new individual side buttons make device control more direct and intuitive."

The Buddha Machine is a truly unique musical device that prefers to sit in the background, quietly and gently working its sonic magic.

*Batteries not included!!!*

items.body:
Genuinely smart art school rock is hard to come by, but Still House Plants make it sound easy, welding subtly R&B-inflected vocals to fractured, free jazz-cum-post rock drums and Shellac-strength axe acrobatics on their incredible third album. Genius, just a bit.

There was a moment during post-rock's evolution when it felt as if the jazz influence that had been simmering in the background since the Talk Talk days was about to bubble over. Tortoise were making firmer connections with Chicago's pantheon of jazz greats, and bands like Boston's Karate were using a music school education to fuel songs that felt kaleidoscopic and open-minded. But as the '90s drew to a close, the genre tightened up and seemed to wander one of two ways: overbearing darkness or luxury car adverts. Still House Plants formed in 2015 at the Glasgow School of Art, and since then have been painstakingly figuring out how to reconcile their web of influences. The backbone is spiky-but-technical US basement rock like Slint or Shellac, but Jessica Hickie-Kallenbach's spine-tinglingly soulful vocals immediately skew the energy, and the band's interest in electronic recording techniques puts them more in line with day zero post-rockers Bark Psychosis. 

They lean into all these contradictions on 'If I don't make it, I love u', infusing their spidery rhythms and angular guitars with illusory production techniques that don't upset the mood, letting the powerful vocals swirl around front of house. Much has been made of the trio's love of UKG, and while that's a potentially lazy reference point, Hickie-Kallenbach's delivery is unmistakably indebted to club music. So much so that the fusion is brilliantly unsettling at first; on 'M M M', she loops late night memories ("I just want my friends to get in!") while David Kennedy thuds jerky rhythms and Finlay Clark phases asymmetric strums. Their process is confident and unique, slipping from cohesion into freeform chaos - the vocal hooks remain, but Kennedy and Clark sound as if they're remixing themselves on the fly: the drums splay into fragments, the guitar layered into tremolo'd wails.

It's easy music to like, the kind of gear that's ambitious without being lofty. You can spot the references, in fact Still House Plants don't bother to cover up their influences, instead feeding off their apparent contradictions in a way that's just a joy to try and suss out even after the umpteenth play. They're just a ridiculously tight band, at the peak of their thing, apparently enjoying every minute of it.

A great album, 10/10.

Remastered for its 1st vinyl cut, The Bug aka Kevin Richard Martin’s immensely forlorn ’22 solo jag immures the senses in a slow-burn blizzard of white-out atonalities and infrasonic rumbles shot thru with an unnerving isolationist melancholia. One hard RIYL Thomas Köner, Mika Vainio’s elemental Ø works, or GAS, gone noxious.

Positively the bleakest thing he’s ever made, ’Sub Zero’ is a supremely powerful listening experience. Thry a dozen tracks Martin pushes the hallmarks of his work, under various guises and collaborations, to a logical conclusion of aesthetic and emotive obliteration. Effectively the heaviest ends of his work as part of EAR (with Porter Ricks’ Mellwig/Köner, Kevin Shields, Pete Kember), the dankest frequencies of The Bug, the detachment of ’Sirens’ (Room 40) and utterly heartbroken qualities of King Midas Sound, are collapsed into the sound of a luscious black hole succour, with a grasp of life-affirming heaviness that dangles it just above the end of the rope. 

Perhaps KRM’s finest, purest hour of aural haunting, the dozen tracks unfurl in glacial streaks on the imagination with a sense of scale and presence that pins heads in place, vulnerable to the elements. He continues to limn the void like he’s lived inside it and survived to tell the tale. A longhand conviction in dub-as-method guides him to the limits of that sound, where it crosses the threshold into realms shared by dark ambient, at the peripheries of BM, post-techno electronics and doom metal. In this atmospheric no-man’s-land he leaves an indelibly ambiguous impression, palpably stricken by existential dread but with pangs of beauty, as in the upswell of Eno-esque choral pads on ‘Too Human’ and ‘Higher Than the Sky’ that cling to hope like a limpet on the hull of his icebreaking structures. 

Magisterial stuff by an artist arguably in his imperial phase.

War.Poem by Chris Connelly, via Dirter Promotions.

“ "WAR.POEM” was recorded at THE ROCK NOIR studio in 2025/2026 as a reaction to a piece I read on the Israeli military use of FLECHETTE SHELLS in Gaza, this led to a much deeper study of the 20th/21st century history of war. The album was composed entirely using a TAPE O MATIC 710 reel to reel from 1958, a 1960’s mayfaair JVC reel to reel, aa 1965 G.E. solid state portable reel to reel from 1965, a portable 1970’s Panasonic cassette player, a ring modulator as well as various other effects and synths.

The loop that is the basis for WAR POEM ZERO which takes up the whole of side one, happened by accident when I put a reel on the wrong way up, it produced aa sound of such great melancholy and beauty, I just let it play…

This album owes a debt to “SWANSONG” by NURSE WITH WOUND from the album “A MISSING SENSE” where experimental sound is used as an anti war protest.

- Chris Connelly 2026"

You are unlikely to hear a record of such brutal intensity, or indeed authenticity as this. To call it “old school industrial” would be to do it a disservice, but also not THAT wide of the mark. It is packaged sympathetically to Chris’ previous release for the label, the long sold out LP “White Phosphorous”."

items.body:
Originally released in 1995, Rachel Goswell and Neil Halstead's Mojave 3 debut 'Ask Me Tomorrow' has finally been given the deluxe treatment - remastered by Abbey Road and back in print for the first time in years. 

It's hard to believe that 'Ask Me Tomorrow' appeared less than a year after 'Pygmalion'. Slowdive's last album flopped at the time, though - their fusion of waved electronica and shoegaze wouldn't really catch on until a few decades later, long after the band had splintered. And in their wake, Halstead and Goswell traded the sounds of deep space for something more earthy, drawing on their love of Bob Dylan and Townes Van Zandt to record a demo of country-tinged acoustic pop. The tape made its way to 4AD's Ivo Watts-Russell, and was quickly bumped up into a full album that's probably the band's most consistently enjoyable. 

Goswell and Halstead sound refreshingly comfortably making echoing, Lynchian alt-country - something that shouldn't be too surprising to anyone who obsessed over the windy, whimsical 'Pygmalion' fave 'Blue Eyed An' Clear'. And they're still trapped in the shadow of shoegaze past on their debut, obscuring their vocals with reverb and slowing their songs down to a sensual crawl. Opener 'Love Songs on the Radio' lies between Slowdive and Mazzy Star and Goswell has rarely sounded better, while Halstead sounds almost like Nick Drake on the charming 'You're Beautiful'. The best is saved for last: 'Mercy', the album's dark, melancholy finale that sounds as if it's waving goodbye to an era that's already disappeared.

items.body:
Lechuga Zafiro, Low Jack, OSSX and Sylvere turn in a suite of remixes for last year's 'Burbujas', Daniel Pineda's first solo EP in almost a decade.

Capturing the essence of Einhundert's legendary parties as well as extending the impact of Pineda's EP, 'Burbujas (Remixes)' quite intentionally surveys the underground club landscape and joins up its landmarks. Paris-based beatmaker Sylvere is up first and pays respect to his roots in the Caribbean with a bouyon version of 'Motif Mambo', switching up its rhythm and interjecting with energetic drops. Then Low Jack weighs in with his twanging version of Pineda's "baby rave" banger 'Siq One' adding a gruesome distorted bassline and chest-crushing gated kicks. Jersey duo (and Einhundert regulars) OSSX drive 'Invocations' through the East Coast with a pneumatic kick-break thrust that's neatly spruced up with vocal slices and rave-ready organ vamps and it's down to the always reliable Lechuga Zafiro to tie a bow around the whole set with an expectedly inventive tribute to DJ Rolando.

2026 has been light on the club highlights, but this one hits the spot.

Essential listening FFO Time Is Away, Jon Collin or the 'Bagpuss' soundtrack, Rory Salter, aka Malvern Brume, confronts cutesy British folk nostalgia on 'For Red Riverbank', using 'The Wind in the Willows' references, sobering newsreel snippets and straight-to-tape acoustic jams to develop a faded image of labour inequality.

Nostalgia is supposed to be digestible - a cultural banana that gives the mind all familiarity without friction. But munch on the same gear for too long and it starts to cause irritation; it's hard not to notice, for example, that the prim Ghost Box-style Gen Z hauntology has reached its logical conclusion. Whatever it was saying about the UK's welfare-era lost futures has not only been photocopied half to death, but it's also been added to the slop machine, spat out as empty "content" that's almost hypnotically nauseating - especially when you consider the state of welfare in 2026. Thankfully, we're not the only people to have noticed; Salter takes aim at the romance of British folk culture on his proper The Sprigs debut, using a framework we'll all be familiar with - Kenneth Grahame's Edwardian children's classic 'The Wind in the Willows'. It's important to note that the book was already steeped in nostalgia when it was first published back in 1908, a reflection on nature in the face of mass industrialization, as the affordable Ford Model T was beginning to appear on roads for the first time. So it's a more complex reference than you might initially figure, and Salter uses this backdrop to root his investigation of British labour history and the very meaning of tradition.

We've all heard remnants of folk music vibrate through the collective consciousness over the years, not least in the wake of the New Weird America movement of the early '00s. And Salter's awareness of these sounds and the perpetual churn that followed is crucial; he doesn't subvert them as such, but repurposes them, hitting on themes and sequences that connect us to the country's soil and textures that help to rub away some of nostalgia's entrancing sparkle. The 12-minute opener 'come along, back home' sounds at first like an old protestant hymn being bellowed through broken pipes and Salter keeps scraping away at history, collaging textured environmental loops with simplistic, almost naive folk songs, peculiar resonances and, occasionally, what sounds like an old recorder. And it's the back-and-forth between gravelly noise and nostalgic naivety that makes 'For Red Riverbank' so inviting. The short, sharp 'Ratty & the moles get to work' is just as jolly as its title, sounding as brittle and evocative as Sandra Kerr and John Faulkner's fluttered folk songs that lifted Oliver Postgate's 'Bagpuss'.

And Salter doesn't just look back through rose-tinted spectacles, he juxtaposes these evocative sounds with sobering recordings of newsreaders, politicians and union leaders, who complete a quite genuine picture of the recent past. Like George Eliot's Middlemarch, that imagined a fictional Midlands town four decades prior to its writing, the inviting idealized setting was a Trojan horse for Eliot's real theme: the 1832 Reform Act that upended the electoral system. Salter employs the same sleight of hand, introducing us to a world we know and love before drip, drip, dripping the politics we so desperately need.

Perhaps the most interesting PAN in a minute; ‘Lila’ is the label debut from Paris-based Algerian Mohamed Bourouissa, best known as a visual artist but now offering a glimpse into his musical practice for the first time, blending highly unusual ambient pulses with autotuned, low-lit vocals, recorded on the fly using a keyboard, mixer, microphone and effects. It runs like some lost 1980’s private press, tipped FFO early Yves Tumor, Yungwebster, Space Afrika, AYYA, Future, Kareem Lotfy.

Bourouissa’s first solo album finds the 48 year old artist capturing the permeable membrane between Paris' various communities through a dream diary of hazed ambient reflections, cloud rap inversions and bass-heavy club malfunctions. It follows his work over decades incorporating music as a phantom thread of his practice in photography, sculpture, and video, and perfectly conveys a sense of longing and melancholy central to Arabic classical and pop songs mediated via an electronic hypermodernism . The album is an intimate, sometimes unsettling experience, aptly described as “hypnagogic” by PAN, as heard in its tendency to dreamlike slowness and the layered haze of FX and xenharmonic chords that shroud and wreath his melismatic woes. 

The dozen tracks play out through autotuned vocal plumes familiar from work by Ayshay, Rainy Miller or Future, crossed with the type of deep blooz oozing from that superb Taymour x Bareetlblad turn on the diy label earlier this year. Each track taps a different pole into the album's landscape, one beatless, and one filled with machinegun toms and explosive snares. The beatless tracks are peculiarly stirring and the heavier, noisier moments somehow vanish into the same aether. Bourouissa peppers the album with wild twists and turns, hitting a dark alley on the anxiety-inducing 'NMB' and descending corrugated steps to a members-only basement on 'MN'. The relief comes with the title track, a collaboration with Fanigliulo (aka Mushy) that's a tender, hopeful moment -  a clouded love song that injects some hope into the darkness.

Special edition of Sun Ra’s classic ‘Lanquidity’, for the 25th anniversary of the label. If yr looking for a way to penetrate Ra's intimidating catalog, "Lanquidity" is a precious wormhole that gives a taste of the jazz pioneer's astral weirdness without letting it overwhelm. Transformative shit, really.

Released in a tiny edition back in 1978, "Lanquidity" is Sun Ra's attempt at cultural reconciliation. It's the ultimate flex, finding the Arkestra alien absorbing contemporary pop elements (disco, funk, soul) into his canon, before spitting them out as further cosmic strings in his pan-universal bow. The playability of "Lanquidity" has given it legs: before its reissue in 2000, the album had hardly been heard, but was spoken about in hushed tones. A couple of decades later, it's an established classic, putting Sun Ra's talent into full view and quieting some of the sprawling galaxy-brain oddness that alienates some listeners.

Recorded by Philly Jazz boss Tom Buchler (who penned enlightening liner notes about the recording experience), "Lanquidity" has Sun Ra fronting a band of over fourteen players, including Marshall Allen on alto sax and John Gilmore on tenor. Intriguingly, he also ropes in not one but two guitarists, giving the album its "Bitches Brew"-adjacent fusion fuzz, but it's the overdubbing of disembodied voices and layers of Arp and Minimoog that puts these tracks into a category all of their own. The mood Sun Ra creates is truly planetary (just flick to the album's terrifyingly tripped 'There Are Other Worlds (They Have Not Told You Of)' for proof) and while he certainly makes concessions with his stylistic choices, the pop shell is merely a Trojan horse for his vanguard forms.

Classic.

items.body:
Jake Muir returns with a new album capturing the sound of Berlin’s church bells and British change ringing, where huge sets of tuned church bells are struck in mathematical sequence, complete with subtle but highly tripped out location recordings of the bell ringers and their environment. If yr into work by Gavin Bryars, Áine O'Dwyer or Philip Corner, this one’s for you.

When he moved from Los Angeles to Germany, Muir's first instinct was to reflect on where he was coming from, imagining a surrogate soundtrack to Hollywood's gay porn underground on 'Bathhouse Blues'. But the longer he was in Berlin, the more he found himself drawn to the municipal soundscape - the kind of sounds that Europeans has been exposed to for so long they no longer registered. Berlin’s regular, monotonous bells were particularly intriguing; ringing out into the street at a scale that was unimaginable in the New World. So Muir began to record the sounds, hopping from church to church to capture not just the ringing itself but the sound of the different spaces - from busy Berlin streets to open parks - to piece together his own sonic portrait of the city, far from sticky dancefloors and booming soundsystems. 

While he was researching the history of bell ringing in Europe, Muir stumbled across the UK tradition of change ringing, where huge sets of tuned bells are struck in mathematical sequence, creating long, constantly varying "changes" that'll be familiar to anyone who's ever ventured near a church on Sunday. Wandering from parish to parish in the UK, Muir was welcomed in by various small teams of campanologists who were surprised an American tourist was even interested. With an unprecedented level of access, he was able to record the bells close up and even capture the interactions between the bell ringers as they responded to the shouted calls that direct the sequences. 

So the two discrete sides of 'Campana Sonans' are created with different concepts in mind; the first, 'Erzklang', finds Muir documenting his new home city and its unique sonic characteristics, while 'Changes' is a Picasso-like examination of British change ringing, drawn from many angles at once. Muir sets the scene with local ambiance on the former, letting the solemn, monastic chimes cut through flapping wings, footsteps, nonchalant whistling and birdsong. We're set down in the city, and the noise disappears almost completely as the sonorous bells take hold. Berlin's incessant tram squeals and provides an accent; Muir stretches out each tone so it undulates like a hum beneath the surface, and coaxes our ears to fill in the gaps. Clean, unprocessed bell sounds criss-cross hissing, noisy textures as Berlin's various neighbourhoods begin to blur into each other like the mid-day walk home after a dizzy, wet weekend.

'Changes' on the flip begins with a callback, echoing the first side with doom-y single bell chimes that Muir polishes with swirled, ghostly resonances. It's the tune-up before the main event; Muir dips to near-silence as human voices prepare us for what we're about to hear, bellowing commands to a full circle of bells that lopes and shimmers, kinked by Muir's gentle guiding hand. To date, he's worked with both environmental recordings and carefully picked samples; but on 'Capana Sonans', he sounds as if he's experimenting with a different methodology. There are concepts pulled from both techniques, but Muir is reacting to music as it exists in an environment, pulling apart an instrument and its history by splaying its tonality and juxtaposing various in-situ sounds. Even if we've heard bell ringing, most of us haven't been up into the bell tower and heard the ringers nattering to each other, or the sub-rupturing bass tones that warble from the gigantic resonators when you're up that close. The effect is like hearing history in a brief reverie; Muir isn't trying to recreate church music, but to bring us closer to an intangible moment in our history. 

Beautiful, thoughtful stuff, right at home on the ace enmossed label next to gurgly, hallucinogenic gear from artists like bad lsd trips and Angelo Harmsworth, but fans of Gavin Bryars' 'The Leeds Bells' or Charlemagne Palestine's 'Bells Studies' should  investigate without delay.

items.body:
Supremely exquisite new album of baroque-pop and dream-spun stylings from emergent Greek harpist-composer Sissi Rada, tipped if yr on the line from Svitlana Nainio to Lena Platonos, CV & Jab to Niecy Blues, Laurie Anderson to Jan Steele & John Cage’s ‘Voices and Instruments’ alltimer​...

‘Nana Butu’ is the deeply impressive 5th solo suite by classically trained string player, Sissi Rada, whose skills have been sought out for record and stage by everyone from Lena Platonos to Brian Eno and Jay Glass Dubs in the past decade. It was with her Stroom debut ‘Aporia’ (2024) that Sissi’s magick really registered with our ears, at least, and since then her captivating blend of virtuosic instrumental tekkerz and hallucinatory sound design palette has been confirmed to these ears/eyes in a former Manchester mortuary and on the divine ‘Demeter In Aexone’ LP for Gomma’s Kryptox subsidiary. Now on a dozen parts bejewelled with extended lines of crystalline melody and unfurling like a waking dream, Sissi doubles down on her music’s transcendent enigma beside a cohort of mutually enchanting spars - Charis Karantzas, Jay Glass Dubs, Oï les Ox, and Theodor Milkov - for a real inception of a record; irrefutable proof of a sorceress at work. 

On sides dealing with the “fragile, tangible world of mortals” and “the cosmic beyond, home to souls and celestial beings”, Sissi assumes a psychopomp role to guide listeners between thematic dualities of life/death, light/dark, waking/dreaming, wth typically low-key yet compelling vision. Never showy, and intimate to uncanny degrees, the album foregrounds her voice more than ever. Variously alloyed with alchemic instrumental touches, and diffused in shapes bent between genres, her voice floats with rare elegance against electro-acoustic contours, variously channelling a sort of avant folk R&B bliss like Clara La San meets Sinead O’Connor on the glyding Reese bass of opener ‘Ave Verum’, or blooming in avant-jazz harmonies like Julee Cruise channelling Alice Coltrane in ‘FOGO’, and that’s only the 1st pair. 

It’s a whole pinch-yourself dream herein, plucking on fantasy theatric strings with ‘Benches’, and coming off like some golden era Hollywood diva in her titular centrepiece. The 2nd half serves to suspend disbelief for the duration, subtly ushering a more unearthly feel with a sublime duet of bittersweet jazz harmony and nagging discordance on ‘MI-MI’, and slipping deep into fantasy realms like Xexa jamming with Meredith Monk on the deliquescent Disney trip ‘FOMO’, before mutual spirit and avant-chanteuse Oï les Ox chimes in on an all-too-short ‘Message’ and it continues to surprise until the end, with the tart vignette ‘Your Order at 4’ calling to mind Beth Gibbons reframed by Rashad Becker, and ‘Wooden Floors’ signs off with a flourish of prepared piano of AFXian virtues. Your ears won’t deceive you - or if they do, in the best way - on this utterly absorbing gem by a real standout in the contemporary field.

All killer, no filler, evergreen compendium of no wave to punk-funk and synth wave from a pivotal era of NYC dance history. Simply too many nuggets to name a fave - a big one for any there at the time, or who got it 2nd hand via LCD Soundsystem and the sound’s whole Y2K resurgence.

‘New York Noise – Dance Music From The New York Underground 1978-82’ was among the most crucial retrospective comps of the early 00's. It would emerge in the wake of LCD Soundsystem’s anthem ‘Losing My Edge’, and an upswell of electroclash to perfectly join the dots between NYC’s late ‘70s, early ‘80s upstarts who adapted punk’s license to bridge rock and dance in mutant new styles which still light a fire under the ass of so many artists bands today, generations later. 

Shake a stick and you’ll hit a minter anywhere across the 16 tunes, from Liquid Liquid’s percolated cowbells on the punk funk blueprint ‘Optimo’ (which lent its title to the legendary club night), to impLOG’s freaky proto-techno bomb ‘Holland Tunnel Dive’, the wiry jump-up chops of The Contortions’ Contort Yourself’, thru the louche synth wave swag of ‘Reduction’ by Bill Laswell’s Material, the no wave yowl of Mars and Theoretical Girls’ stop/start torque, to Alan Vega ov Suicide’s rock ’n roll throwback, ‘Bye Bye Bayou’.

The Congos’ Lee “Scratch” Perry-produced and mixed roots evergreen is one you’d play to aliens enquiring about reggae. It returns to vinyl orbit with VP Records for the umpteenth time, primed for any shelf - as essential as they come.

It’s hard to overstate the classic status of ‘Heart of the Congos’, which was recorded at Lee Perry’s legendary Black Ark in 1977, and has endured as a staple of the reggae canon ever since. The trio of “Ashanti” Roy Johnson (tenor), Cedric Myton (falsetto) and Watty Burnett (baritone) harmonise heavenly - notably backed by likes of Gregory Isaacs, The Heptones, and The Meditations - on rhythms laid down by crack players including Sly Dunbar, all spangled with Perry’s signature production and mix magick, hailing the wee madman at a crest of his creativity. Then fresh from massive success with Max Romeo and Junior Murvin for Island Records, Perry’s legal wrangling with Island meant The Congos’ album was issued via his Black Ark, limiting its global reach, and as such it was a cult burner until constant reissues assured its place in the reggae pantheon by end of the century.

Fair to say we were properly bitten by The Congos circa Blood & Fire’s ‘Fishermen Style’ album of versions by Horace Andy, Big Youth, Sugar Minott and many more in 2006, largely due the fact they were our office neighbours and you couldn’t get in to work without hearing it, accompanied by a waft of bush weed, during that year. As such, the beatific harmonies of its swaying lead cut are hard imprinted on memory, and gave us a lil shiver when hearing it mixed in the air over the rooftops of Whalley Range during recent carni. Together with the peppery, machine-driven lilt of ‘Congoman’ (also available on deadly Carl Craig edit), the sublime stepper ‘Can’t Come In’, and Lee Perry leaning into the deepest vein of spooky roots reggae soul on ‘Ark of Covenant’, the whole thing is a best in class example of Jamaican songcraft and dance innovation in the late ’70s, finely balancing groove, mood, and some Xth factor of psychedelic, soul-tingling brilliance that hits like little else.

On their second album, Chicago underground staples Eric Block and Bruce Lamont, alongside ex-Sonic Youth drummer Steve Shelley, recruit Tortoise's Douglas McCombs for a packed session of krautrock-inspired avant jazz rock.

Sick Gazelle's debut album 'Odum' was the result of pure happenstance, when Shelley just happened to join Block and Lamont for a last-minute jam. It was good enough to launch an entire project and seven years later, the trio have invited bassist McCombs to fill out their sound. And it's his plodding basslines that finish off the sound; each of the five tracks started life as an improvisation, gradually sculpted by repetition to play to the band's strengths. Needless to say, if you're interested in Chicago's jazz-inspired improv rock scene, 'Vield' will offer you plenty to chew on. Where else are you gonna find a nine-minute track called 'Ocean Always Wins' that sounds as if the guitars are literally drowning the rest of the instruments? Exactly.

items.body:
A perennial reminder to the raw-ass bluesy soul house stomp and wiggle of the GOATy two-part debut album by Detroit/Chicago legend Theo Parrish.

Now of a 28 year vintage, the ultimate collection of woodcut drums, burnished keys and soul-fired vibes in ‘First Floor’ (1998) have aged like a cask oak-steeped single malt whiskey. It’s now a contemporary classic touchstone for deep house at its earthiest and most spirited, depicting Theo locked into signature offbeat grooves that have buried themselves deep under the skin and soundtracked countless late night soirées.

Future-proofed by its uniquely loose but taut knit of minimalist elements worked to jazzwise, hypnotic effect, you can practically taste the sweet smoke and tang in the air of each cut, spanning the lip-bitingly strong, heads-down hustle of ‘First Floor Metaphor’ at the front, thru the timeless deep house immanence of ’Sky Walking’ at the back. In between, ‘Sweet Sticky’ works nagging organ vamps and nattiest drums into a proper stank-face trample, next to the honeyed chords of ‘Paradise Architects’, classic sampler magick in ‘Love Is war For Miles’, a ‘JB’s Edit’ for the wall-bangers, and 10 mins of limb-unravelling tekkerz on ‘Dark Patterns’. Plus, obviously ‘Heal Yourself & Move’ the deepest alltimer, a track that feels almost like a second skin at this point.

It’s one of those albums that’s truly transcends generic borders to influence heads of all stripes with its unmistakeable, soul-nuzzling texture and groove. One for the ages, we tell thee.

So this is a bit special… thanks to the efforts of a NIN forum, Coil's legendary and incredible 'Recoiled' versions of Nine Inch Nails are finally given an official release.

Although never properly released - other than excerpts used in David Fincher's Se7en - the tracks have been in circulation for some years now yet never collected for a full release like this. It includes five extended and thorough revisions of some total NIN classics in just under 40 minutes, all crafted in the pre-Ableton era and ranging from a gutted and strung out version of 'Closer [Unrecalled]' - as used in Se7en - to a blinding deconstruction of 'The Downward Spiral [A Gilded Sickness]', to an extended and industrialized take on 'Gave Up [Open My Eyes]', and two reworks of 'Eraser' - a beatless 'Reduction', and a previously unheard, technoid 'Baby Alarm' mix with bespoke effects crafted from, you guessed it, a baby alarm.

For many, it's debatable whether this is what the late great Peter Christopherson and Jhonn Balance would have wanted - as with all their posthumous releases and reissues - but it's really hard to argue when the thing is in your hands. Highly recommended.

One of Masami Akita's most unexpected collaborations, 'Strange City' is surprisingly legit, pieced together from licensed samples and framed by Akita's visceral distortions.

You have to wonder how it might have sounded if Sun Ra and Akira had come face to face, but 'Strange City' is about as close as we'll get. An official release made with the blessing of Irwin Chusid, executor of the Sun Ra catalog, the album was made from "rare and unreleased tracks from the Sun Ra archive", which Akita puts through the meat grinder, as expected.

What we actually hear from those original recordings is tough to gauge. On 'Livid Sun Loop', there's a burst of drums and horn for a few moments before the squeals are snuffed out almost completely by Akita's own shrieking white noise. Soon, the sounds are buried beneath dense layers of distortion and fritzed oscillations - audible if you train your attention to cut between the wall of noise, but left as a trace, followed by Akita. 

On the epic flip 'Granular Jazz Pt. 2', Akita allows more room for Sun Ra's recordings, paring down his blaring cacophony to a soft racket and allowing the horns and rattling drums to at least interact with his arsenal of machines. Now that's jazz.

items.body:
After crafting an all-timer with 2008's 'Hazyville', Actress set his sights on the unknown with a futureshock debut for Honest Jon's.

Wheras it's predecessor was composed over a staggered period of many years, Splazsh was fashioned in a fraction of that time, lending a tangible symmetry between shapeshifting tracks that defined and propelled the era. Of the 14 tracks, we'd previously encountered the first two, with the unstable space float of 'Hubble' appearing on a shady Thriller 12" and his remix of Various Production's 'Lost' reminding us that there are some deep cuts in the Cunningham discography.

From here in it's all about that longing, sealing the airlock and initiating pressure sequence with 'Futureproofing', before laying down 'Always Human' - can u even remember a time you didnt know this one? Showing resistance towards any categorisation, 'Get Ohn (Fairlight Mix)' swerves down a side street into a footwurkin' face-off by sliding to a mutilated mix of Jon E Cash and Chez Damier played underwater. Next we hit the erogenous interzone of 'Maze' and that incapacitatingly lush bassline designed to lock into your central nervous system and send shockwaves of piloerection to every fucking corner of your soul.

After that, we're cynically dumped into the Ferraro-esque Prince tribute 'Purple Splazsh', and on into the Detroit ghetto stalk of 'Let's Fly'. The dissonant robo-crunk of 'The Kettle Men' and closing entry 'Casanova' confirm that if anything, Actress only suffers from a surfeit of ideas. Proof, if it were needed, that there is a sprawling future beyond the stasis of so much contemporary electronic music.

items.body:
First re-pressing in years of Mark Ernestus & Moritz Von Oswald’s divine, final Rhythm & Sound release, heeling to tradition with a one-riddim album focussed on its carousel of roots reggae legends; Sugar Minott, Paul St. Hilaire, Willi Williams, Jah Cotton, Bobbo Shanti, and more

In 2005 Rhythm & Sound capped their holy mountain catalogue with ‘See Mi Yah’, a 7 x 7” set and LP which completed a 10 year run of inspired dub productions with their purest offering to the form. At the time, younger ears to their music would be left perplexed by the lack of instrumental variation - but any others with a little knowledge of one-riddim set traditions knew it was their ultimate ode to roots reggae fundamentals, after respectfully messing with the style & pattern across the Burial Mix 10”s (as collected in ‘w/ The Artists’), and the more radical 12” mutations of the Rhythm & Sound series, proper, since 1996 (not to mention birthing dub house-techno before that).     

Seeing off the project in fine style, Ernestus & Von Oswald gave studio time to their favourite vocalists, generating a slew of original performances displaying the range and depth of roots reggae’s elders and contemporary torch carriers on their signature backdrop of air-trodding bass and powdered dub chords. We were blessed to distribute it in the UK at the time, so many of these cuts are hard etched to the memory, from the ghostly croon of Willi Williams’ title piece thru the gruff gravitas of Bobbo Shanti, the duet between Ras Donovan & Ras Perez, and of course Sugar Minott’s mellifluous reggae soul.

In the year following ‘See Mi Yah’, Rhythm & Sound were naturally elected to edit and master a re-up of The Congos & Friends’ one-riddim album ’Fisherman Style’ for our then warehouse neighbours Blood & Fire Records, sealing their era of roots reflection by appropriately saluting the originators, in parallel to their Wackies reissue scheme, and before Ernestus (and Mark Ainley) would go on to found the more digi-devoted reissue label, Dug Out. Some 20 years of satisfaction later, time has proven this album holds its meditative weight.

items.body:
Sing Forever (Singing Is Free): Songs from 2021-2023 was initially released as a seven song cassette that came with early copies of A Profound Non-Event. Now with the addition of an extra song and a remastering by Mikey Young, it is now released as a limited 12" LP via Tough Love.

"Sing Forever (Singing Is Free): Songs from 2021-2023 meets us as a foreword to A Profound Non-Event, Daily Toll's debut album from 2025. Offering an earlier chapter in the ever-growing songbook of the Sydney/Gadigal-based group, Sing Forever... is a collection in demo-form that maps their initial formative period as a duo, largely marked by Covid-era isolation, diabolical housemates, sonic experiments and copious amounts of wine sourced from Kata's job at the time.

As bowerbirds of song, Kata and Jasper are making sounds from their own pocket - their world! - singing from nowhere to no-one from (in) a context of global upheaval, loss and mass confusion. Here we find the urge to sing forever, to share a morsel of spirit, and with it a mode of grounding one's humanity. The songs are loose, off-beat and textural, a period of "first thought, best thought" in boundless practice that finds inspiration from all over: a bracelet and a solo afternoon in Budapest; lyrics formed via a black-out poem scrawled across the page of a Neil Young biography; the scratch of paper daisies, toy drums, typewriters, and pots and pans all welcome melodies repeating and fumbling unto themselves until ultimately falling apart and into something else.

These songs were never initially intended to find a physical release or to even be distributed further than the Bandcamp void, and yet here we arrive at a kind of essence of Daily Toll, or at least one iteration thereof, before the studio, before the additional band members, and before being known (perhaps, even loved) by more beyond."

items.body:
Numero digs up a full suite of demos from proto slowcore heroes Codeine's 1992 "Barely Real" sessions. One for the heads.

If you peeped Numero Group's bumped-up 2012 reissue of "Barely Real", you might already be familiar with the Dessau mythology. When Codeine were attempting to record their influential 1990 debut album "Frigid Stars" they embarked on a series of sessions that failed to generate enough coherent material for a complete album - tracks that would end up making up the "Barely Real" EP. And after a Sub Pop-funded jaunt in Manhattan and a cheaper session in Allston near Boston, they began recording in New York City again at Harold Dessau Recording Studio. Vocalist Stephen Immerwahr was unhappy with the tracks: he wasn't content with his vocals, wanted to dub the songs at even slower tempos and heard high pitched noises in the recordings. 

Listening now, it's tough to hear exactly what Immerwahr was concerned with - the tracks sound as good as the versions that eventually ended up on "Barely Real" and at times are barely discernible from the finished article. Fans will no-doubt be interested in hearing the complete session (only four of these tracks made it to the "Barely Real" re-release and the "When I See The Sun (Demos & Live Cuts)" compilation), but this probably isn't essential for casual listeners.

items.body:
Decades into a career that began at Paris's fabled GRM, Argentinian innovator Beatriz Ferreyra is still worlds ahead, transmuting environmental recordings and snake-like foley rustles into cosmological whispers that ponder the universe's big questions. 

Commissioned by the French state, "Senderos de luz y sombras" (or pathways of light and shadow) is the latest transmission from Beatriz Ferreyra, who composed the half-hour, 16-channel piece between 2016 and 2020. She was inspired by astrophysics (specifically the time before the Big Bang), and the world of the unconscious mind, and dedicates the composition to the memory of sound sculptor Bernard Baschet, electro-acoustic innovator Bernard Parmegiani, and her friend Carlos Pellegrino. 

If you've heard her  GRM releases, or Room40's two essential anthologies ("Echos+" and "Canto+"), then you'll no doubt already be intrigued - that material helped to cement Ferreyra's well-deserved place in the canon, her work speaks for itself. Ferreyra's fathoms-deep tape manipulation experimentation has inspired countless artists, from Keith Fullerton Whitman and Jim O'Rourke to Debit and Valerio Tricoli, and this latest full-length just reminds us how open-minded and freely experimental her compositions can be.

The piece is split into two side-long chunks, both of which tremble with eerie uncertainty. 'Senderos abismales' is gusty and effortlessly psychedelic, using carved-up field recordings to suggest familiarity before sending us wheezing into the cosmos. Ferreyra doesn't need much: the distinct sounds of tyres on wet tarmac, wind whispering in the distance, and distant birdsong are sculpted into a giddy, multidimensional lattice of chiseled sonics and ponderous philosophy. Her confidence is key here, and she never needs to do too much; the negative space is just as important as any chaotic moments, and the tiny breaths of harmony - from icy winds, spectral processing, or something else entirely - sound as if they're provoking life in a vacuum. Comparatively 'Senderos del olvido' is more upbeat, beginning with exploded star sound design that shifts thru a sci-fi spectrum without using any of the usual pneumatic sound effects that have become customary.

Ferreyra is too thoughtful to rest on obvious cultural totems. Her vision of cosmic emptiness is strikingly human; when she voyages into the abstract, her gurgling, digitally-reduced textures only remind us of the soul behind the complex processes. And just as her '70s tape music allowed us to feel an emotional connection to music that was too often lost in academia's back rooms, "Senderos de luz y sombras" reminds us that the same is true of contemporary computer music. If you enjoyed the run of recent Roland Kayn reissues, this one's gonna be absolutely required listening.

items.body:
The latest Portraits GRM pairs French electro-acoustic artist Eve Aboulkheir with veteran Norwegian polymath Lasse Marhaug. Aboulkheir's side is a dream-diary made from detuned, spiralling oscillations, and Marhaug's is a heartstopping fusion of grim analog ambience. Unmissable!

Aboulkheir's piece was shaped by the swirling sounds, smells and visuals of a visit to China, and the feeling she had of intense perceptual disorientation crossing markets, as if walking through a dream. Using advanced electro-acoustic techniques to represent a near-psychedelic mindset, the piece feels almost completely weightless, haunting the sonic space as it whirls and whirrs with the grace of a marionette guided by invisible strings. Aboulkheir composes with a hardy narrative sense - every sound has its place. In just a few minutes, she weaves perplexing snatched voices that reverberate into dissociated micro-voids and dissolved field recordings. There might be a crash or splash of water, before obsessively tweaked and edited synths form their own cyber-lingual chirps and babbles. When Aboulkheir introduces percolating rhythms at the halfway point, it's just another confounding colour; the whisper of club music is there in the distance, obscured by walls, bodies and geography. We can hear parallels with Jim O'Rourke, Ben Vida, Delia Derbyshire (think 'Blue Veils and Golden Sand') and the great Morton Subotnick - basically if you're interested in hearing the potential of modern electro-acoustic music, it’s a must-listen.

Lasse Marhaug's 'How to Avoid Ants' is stylistically different, but just as narratively driven as its predecessor. Using concréte techniques, Marhaug recreates his daughters journey to forest camp, avoiding the anthills lining the path along the way. He mulches the sound of creaking tree branches and rustling leaves into rich guitar drones and synthesised groans, carefully suggesting force, texture and volume even through the most hushed passages. The opening moments almost feel like Deathprod's tenebrous early material, with brain-tickling organic foliage sounds on top of doomed, steely strings. When his patented sheet noise creaks into the frame, it's at arm's length, whooshing like a kettle on the River Styx, over rumbling, indistinct sub-bass rumbles. Marhaug never lets it boil over, instead pulling back to reveal creeping wintery pads, leading into bells that come out of nowhere and add a full stop to a piece of music that’s fully captivating over its 17 minute duration.

Sferic/Faitiche emissary Roméo Poirier pairs up with stylistic mentor Jan Jelinek on a sampler's delight, answering Jelinek's romantic 2005 gem 'Collage of Digital Passion' with a montaged mirror image that fizzes with plunderphonic warmth.

Jelinek has been using The Exposures pseudonym since 2003, most notably pillaging micro-samples from numerous R&B records on "Collage Of Digital Passion” issued by Prefuse 73’s Eastern Developments label back in 2005. In his by-now inimitable loop-finding style, that track has become a bit of a low-slung classic, reminding us not only of his iconic productions of the early 2000’s, but also of Anthony Shakir’s iconic ‘Mr. Shakir's Beat Store’ from just a couple of years earlier.

For his “version”, Poirier flips “I hate you!" samples with fanciful, theatrical soundscapes that ooze warmth, capturing the essence of Jelinek's original perfectly.

Formally known as Rabbitfoot, 1000 Rabbits survey their first months and years of activity on this brittle six-track EP.

Since they first assembled in Aldeburgh two years back, 1000 Rabbits have tracked from living room to rehearsal space to stage, working through ideas and concepts to come up with a tight selection of experimentally-minded art pop that should appeal to fans of Wet Leg and Black Country New Road. If you've come across the band before, you've probably run into 'Virgin Soil' a featherlight fusion of staccato string plucks, time signature switches and orchestral swells that sits at odds with vocalist River's nonchalant recollections. 'Rubiks Cube' expands the concept a little more, adding a proggy synth low-end and more elaborate drumming, but it's the non singles that convince us that 1000 Rabbits are more than a novelty name. Peep the gossamer 'Bear Hunt', that sounds as if it coulda come from Clarissa Connelly's 'World of Work', or the lengthy, folk-flecked finale 'Spring Cleaning'.

items.body:
The entwined timelines of Bristol, Africa, and Peter Gabriel’s WOMAD festival and Real World label, manifest across eight previously unreleased, early ’80s jams by a mix of West African, Jamaican and Avon-based musicians, at best in the polyrhythmic groovers by Ben Baddoo International, and an unusual sort of proto-trip hop fusion by Bhundu Boys frontman, Biggie Tembo, with Startled Insects, who would go on to key work with Massive Attack and Madonna...

“It’s more than a special moment when you discover music you’ve never heard (of) before or ever knew existed. 1982 was a critical spark for the development of wider (world) musical styles, both in Bristol and the UK at large. The central event from that year was the first WOMAD festival, held in the unlikely surroundings of the agricultural themed Bath and West Showground near Shepton Mallet in Somerset.

One common thread in Bristol to all of these discoveries was the Ekome Dance Company and most notably Artistic Director, Barrington ‘Barry’ Anderson. Barry had also recruited musicians from African countries such as Cameroon and Ghana, from Jamaica and others from the Bristol area. This was to form the Ekome Arts Band which would offer music with either a specific African or Caribbean focus.

This kickstarted a process and practice in the West Country city where musicians brought over from African countries would collaborate with those from the locality. It is those activities - a sound clash and culture clash, producing material of real depth - that constitute the three different combinations, along with one connection originating in London, that make up material on the first The Bristol Meets Africa Music Sound album, released on Bristol Archive Records.”

We can't tell you who Ferries are, but the band clearly have chops. It's nothing you won't have heard before, sure, but it ain't half nicely done.

Rattly, stripped-to-the-bone IDM gear that harks back to simpler times, BOT1500's second proper album is simple and elegant, more concerned with the emotional weight of its melodies than the complexity of its beats.

You might remember Shinichi Koboyashi's last BOT1500 album 'Surreal', that appeared back in 2022 on AD93's Lith Dolina sublabel. And since then he's been relentlessly prolific on his Bandcamp, issuing regular single track updates that chart his creative process. But 'The Black Sea' is his first longer set in a while, assembling a handful of tracks that highlight his recent interest in minimalism, emotion and dub production techniques. The familiar monosynth groans and dry, jazzy breaks on 'Abstract Springs' might resemble Squarepusher for a moment, but it's much chillier, sparser gear, with space around each element that softens the impact of the hyperactive edits. And on 'Shadows', that same mood pervades the track even when the beats have been silenced; Koboyashi gives just as much importance to his chiming analog synths, coaxing out fragile melodies that sound as if they've been plucked out of time.

And there's a precision to his programming that's immediately impressive. On 'XB 1', his soft focus glitches and woody hits graze the post-dubstep landscape but subtly reframe it, setting the meticulous rhythms against echoing single note sine hits and melancholy pads. And the track's sequel 'XB 2' is an even harder punch to the gut, with exquisite melodies and knife-edge drums that shuttle us right back to 1996 for a moment, an underground dominated by Clear Records, Spymania and Rephlex.

items.body:
Mojave 3's final album, released in 2006, 'Puzzles Like You' is a slick, sunny break from their reverberating early albums.

Undoubtedly the most controversial album in Rachel Goswell and Neil Halstead's Mojave 3 catalog, 'Puzzles Like You' didn't feel exactly like the end of an era when it appeared, but the start of a new one. By this time in the band's evolution, the traces of Slowdive had completely disappeared - which made it all the more surprising when the band re-formed in 2014, effectively ending Mojave 3 for good.

Going back now though, knowing how everything worked out, it's interesting to hear how Goswell and Halstead were motivated to keep up with a shifting industry, reacting to indie's forward motion by kissing goodbye to shoegaze mere moments before they'd become flavor of the month again.

A trenchant UK steppas dub masterpiece, 1993, mercifully returns to vinyl for the first time in over 30 years. Pure soundsystem tungsten produced by TNT Roots and Winston Dread, with OG copies known to trade for triple figures, making this remastered edition a no brainer.

As regularly deployed by Aba Shanti-I and Iration Steppas sounds - both titans in their field - Earthquake Studio’s ‘Dub Harder Than Steel’ is a definitive lodestone of UK digi-dub; a distinctive mutation of the original JA style, seeded on blighty by descendants of the Windrush generation. The sound’s influence resonates deeply with the roots of so much dance music that we hold close to heart on this island - jungle/D&B, UKG, dubstep, and beyond - leading, over time, this particularly platter to be hailed a true holy grail. 

Cooked up on a relatively basic array of a DK-80 synth, Yamaha keyboard, Casio RZ-1 drum machine, and an Atari 1040 computer running Cubase V2.0, Earthquake Studio’s innovative sorcery is found in the way they spatialise and massage the machines’ frequencies to inimitably mystic, transcendent, propulsive effect. Subs go lower than the Dead Sea and natty melodies ring out like reedy sirens according to a unique democracy of the frequency spectrum that really comes into its own with just amplification. Trust laptop speakers will not suffice; you need a proper rig to get the best out of this one: the bigger, the better.

Echoing the likes of Jah Shaka’s ‘Commandments of Dub’ precedents, but in a digickal style & pattern in step with the times, and even more concentrated to fundamentals, ‘Dub Harder Than Steel’ is as good as it gets for the type of proper gut-rumble, nose-flare, heavy troddin’ pressure whose impact can be heard across UK soundsystem music, especially the sort of stuff practised by Digital, Muslimgauze, DMZ, or Raime.

Don’t sleep!

New dance music experiences by mischievous ravers, Two Shell, who pick up and twirl SOPHIE’s hyperpop baton and traces of Basement Jaxx’s classic party starters on 13 fruity big room and club boosters

Love them or loathe them, Two Shell have come to define UK dance in the 2020s at its slipperiest and most playful, skewing and reassembling classic and contemporary conventions with a ludic bent and signature sound design. ‘Infinite Now+’ neatly sustains the sugar-rush of their eponymous debut LP of ’24, and ‘IIcons’ (2025), with sharper focus on vocals and upfront club effect that translates equally well to radio and earbuds, thanks to the duo’s feel for obsessive production detail, arranged with exacting dance-pop concision. In contrast to, say, the Overmono album, Two Shell succeed in a similar arena of big scale events thanks to their measures of playfulness and subtle trippy, psychoacoustic mixing chicanery that lands just the right side of cheesy and is a strange pleasure to revel in.

The alco-popped fizz of ‘Step Inside’ sets out their stall somewhere adjacent to French touch filter house and garage-disco with belting, era-appropriate diva vox, before the album twists off into its shiny permutations: the dubstep-lite R&B pop of ‘The Nightmare’; frothed-up electro-pop patently skooled by SOPHIE on ‘Live Forever’ and ‘Lost in the Sound’; overeasy meat-market disco house in ‘Lose Control’; a sort of speedy G spin on warbling EDM pop with ‘Love You So Much’; louche garage hip-house compressed to weirdly heady effect in ‘Come Alive’; a closing belter, ‘Dance’ recalling Jonny L’s chops for Dane Bowers & Victoria Beckham, or S Club’s ‘Seeing Double’ (2002) album.

items.body:
Coil’s debut live show, proper, and its follow-up, are finally available on 2LP via Thighpaulsandra’s label, Retractor - nearly 2 hours in the mesmerising, in-the-moment presence of their era’s most fêted, esoteric unit.

In the glistening wake of a reissue to ‘Black Antlers’ comes this documentation of Jhonn Balance, Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson, Thighpaulsandra and Ossian Brown, performing live as Coil at the behest of fellow psychonaut Julian Cope for his 2-day event ‘Cornucopea’ at The Royal Festival Hall, South Bank, London, April 2nd 2000, and a few months later at Sónar Festival, Barcelona. Originally issued on 2CD in summer 2003, the London portion is also similar to Coil Presents Time Machines - a bonus disc to ‘Musick To Play in the Dark Vol.2’ - with the whole set representing the first genuine Coil live effort, give or take or few “abortive” early attempts in the early 1980s. 

Bedecked in “fluffy polar Teletubby suits” designed by Jhonn with Nicola Bowery (wife and creative partner of Leigh Bowery) and Ossian Brown, the band would yield a more sensuously liquified iteration of the Time Machines set, already regarded as one of their trippiest, and here smudged to a deeply narcotic efficacy that must have sounded incredible in situ, as it does on the recording, with John’s reserved vox laced to sustained, helical spumes of skin-crackling electronics on the London part. The Sónar recording differs in its more broken structure, allowing for pulsating rhythms rather than weightless, deferred gratification, and leading into pockets of black hole absorption and ultimately a manic climax.

items.body:
Peak Oil boss Brian Foote and scene veteran Paul Dickow (aka Strategy) work at the intersection of classic electronic music, dub techno, city pop and bleep techno on 'High Cube', plowing decades of experience into a taut set of highly atmospheric and jazzwize downtempo grooves. RIYL Move D, Lifted, The Detroit Escalator Co., Purelink.

Longtime pals Dickow and Foote have worked together in various outfits for decades, but somehow never recorded as a duo until now. For ‘High Cube’ they set themselves strict parameters, allowing themselves five bits of gear and one hour to create each track, leaning into the constraints to yield maximum creative energy. 

The album's spontaneous flow is powered by rickety beatbox loops, emotive synth sequences and levitational pads that point to a classic, jazzwize era of electronic music and especially the Detroit-influenced diamonds Dave Moufang produced as Move D and as part of Reagenz, Studio Pankow and Conjoint in the mid 1990’s. It’s all elevated, atmospheric and uplifting, spiralling synth lines dissolved into the airiest production style - an almost naive retro-futurism that feels pure and almost hopeful three decades on from the OG’s.

Peep the free-flowing blips and throbbing bassline on 'Underwater Welder' that the duo season with distorted FM growls and cycling, slo-mo beats, or the weightless, mytho-tropical mood they evoke with just a few elements on the hypnotic 'A Dragon's Treasure is its Soul'.

Maybe they do make them like they used to, after all.

The 1977 version was conceived by Jazz man Jun Arasaki and his group Nine Sheep, and executed in one take (this recording) on five sanshin, four winds, piano, bass, percussion and drums for a TV broadcast. It’s somehow solemn yet joyous in a slow and stately way, with lyrics describing how “beautiful buds unfold”.

Fourth World inhabitants and dreamers Visible Cloaks remix ‘Kajyadhi Fu Bushi’ in their own image, resulting a diaphanous, gauzy swell of harmonised synth chorales infiltrated by playful ghosts in the machine and weft with elusive traces of the original vocal to sound like a Google deep dream reverie of the real thing.

items.body:
Retrospective of elegant rare groove and folk-pop from Phnom Penh’s golden age of sound in the 1960s and 1970s.

"In those vibrant years, the city pulsed with music: rock bands, crooners, and traditional ensembles blended East and West, shaping a uniquely Cambodian pop that shimmered with hope and modernity. Amid this flourishing scene, So Savoeun’s voice stood out—silken yet powerful, intimate yet expansive, carrying with it the promise of a new era. This collection brings together rare and long-unheard recordings, including luminous duets with legendary contemporaries Meas Saman, Lek Savath, and Sinn Sisamouth.

Each track is more than just a song—it is a fragment of memory, a preserved echo of nights when Phnom Penh’s dance halls and radios overflowed with rhythm and possibility. In her own words, hearing these songs resurface is like opening a long-buried chest of jewels, hidden beneath the dust of history and now gleaming again after half a century. Her voice, once thought lost to time, reemerges like the cicada whose chant reverberates endlessly through the forest—an eternal call that bridges silence and remembrance. Her music is more than nostalgia; it is testament and rebirth. It continues to resonate, not only with those who lived through that golden era, but with new generations discovering its beauty for the first time. Through this release, the past breathes again—tender, luminous, and unforgettably alive."

items.body:
Vaporwave catalyst Spencer Clark (The Skaters) responds to the paintings of Belgium-based Croat artist Vedran Kopljar with some of his lushest, worm-holing, inter-dimensional synth trips.

Some 15 years since the first instalment of The Spectacle of Light Abduction, Clark takes cues from Kopljar’s vividly surrealistic windows of invention to dive headlong into polychromatic alleys of the mind. A sense of ceremonial ritual emerges in passage from the herded rhythms and aeolian winds of ‘Abyssfields’ into the high plains drift evoked by ‘Abomination Plateaus’, adapting prevailing winds of new age ambient and Troma-esque synth gunk to put a proper breeze behind one’s noumenal sails and leave lots to the imagination. Trust it’s not the corny signposted pish that vaporwave has become, but a visionary, world-building immersion in Clark’s magnificent inner world, a place familiar yet strangely displaced from normality, where the synths exhale pure DMT-like fractals and tickle atavistic reaches of the amygdala.

items.body:
Future modal jazz dub, heard thru a Y2K lens by legendary blowers Pharaoh Sanders & Graham Haynes, and diffused in Bill Laswell’s illbient dub style & pattern. A slept-on, cross-generational ace sure to pique interest FFO Jon Hassell to Talvin Singh, Lászlo Hortobágyi to Material.

Cooked up in NYC’s jazz crucible in 2003 as a duo of Sanders & Haynes - now re-mantled as a Sanders x Laswell session for its first vinyl cut - ‘With a Heartbeat’ speaks to the rich confluence of deeply rooted, forward-thinking jazz with ambient dub that tilted from the late C.20th into this century. Centred on the human heartbeat, it unfurls at a rested systolic throb in two landscaped-scale works which bookend deeper dives into Indian raga and tabla actions, the latter of which may find favour on open-minded ‘floors, due to its effortless, toes-off-the-ground levity. But essentially, it’s idealised for floating at home or road tripping on the astral highway.

Bill Laswell’s name at the top signifies his integral input, but with no discount to Graham Hayne’s cornet, beautifully knit in warm, rising air with his peer, pioneering tenor sax player Pharaoh Sanders, who brings a half century of chops with Coltrane, Sharrock, and myriad others, to the plate. Quite simply it’s a lush listen from front to back, opening from heartical subbass pulse into 17 mins of dusted illbient dub with a cool reserve on ‘Across Time’, and shoring up in almost big beat 4th world fusion scapes reminding of the eL-Hortobãgyi Hortator album with ‘Gamaka’.

Yet we’re most partial to the midsection, where Sanders & Haynes colour the luxuriant space and rolling ballast with a wider range of brass and woodwind in the dewy raga of ‘Morning Tala’, and Trilok Gurtu’s undulating and spicy tabla and scatting vox evoke an aerial game of hashed-out kabaddi in ‘Alankara’.

items.body:
Autechre's reissue engine reaches their outstanding 2008 album, featuring definitive moments of their near 40 year (and ongoing) run.

‘Quaristice’ is Rob Brown and Sean Booth’s 9th studio album as Autechre, conceived some 20 years up-to-the-hilt in their thing, and depicting the duo emerging into a sort of hybrid live x studio jam style that’s distinguished much of their work thus far. However archänlèy, it’s still not even the best version - that honour is reserved to the 2.5hr digital-only ‘Quaristice.Quadrange.ep.ae’ brimming with extended versions, including an hour long mix of ‘Perlance subrange 6-36’ and deadly 10’ mix of ‘Tkakanren’ - but suffice it to say we’re made up to see this one in the wild on vinyl, at least.

The follow-up to a pivotal standout, 2004’s ‘Untilted’ (also reissued this year), ‘Quaristice’ really felt like a future upgrade to the system on its release in 2008. Completely unconcerned with prevailing or emerging trends of dubstep or UKF at the time, it sees the duo follow their noses for hardware/ software jams into the proper mutant body music, milling limbs to the meanest 112BPM electro swag in the twin-rotor electro hip hop gnash of ‘Tankakern’, and utterly wrecking the senses in the blizzard dynamic of ‘Fol3’, or manipulating sinew with deviant liquid B-Boy tekkerz on ’90101-5l-l’ - each of which feature in even better versions on the 2nd disc (and frankly better yet in their alternative extensions of the digi-only version). 

There are flashes of the melodic and harmonically curious Autechre we all know and love in opener ‘Altibzz’ (their love note to the magic of Altrincham), the aerated strings of ‘Theswere’, and almost Lynchian noir of ‘Notwo’, yet the whole thing feels to trigger muscle memories and flashbacks to club physicality, as felt in the corresponding live show at Pure in Manchester at the time. The mad thing is, as judged from recent live show, they still sound as rudely uncompromising and propulsive now, 17 years later, perhaps more than ever

items.body:
Mojave 3's dreamy sophomore album, originally released in 1998, returns to 4AD with a brand new lick of paint from its Abbey Road remaster.

By the time 'Out of Tune' was release, shoegaze felt like a distant memory. Even Britpop's dominant influence had started to fade by this stage: Pulp released 'This Is Hardcore' and post-rock bubbled into a rolling boil, Slowdive had become an afterthought. But Mojave 3 were surprisingly popular, their impeccably written alt-country snatching fans from Tindersticks and Hope Sandoval. Sadly, 'Out of Tune' wasn't quite as ineffably beautiful as their debut, marked by clarity as Halstead moved further away from the Slowdive sound and ditched the reverb completely, but it's still worth a look.  

'Some Kinda Angel' is an engaging duet that highlights the power of their swelled lineup (with Simon Rowe joining on electric guitar and Alan Forrester on organ and piano). And 'Yer Feet' is between Radiohead and Leonard Cohen - a minimal slow burner that shows just how good Halstead was at writing simple, effective songs.

Emotional Response presents the first of 2 EPs by Laura Sparrow aka LNS, the Calgary raised, Berlin based producer and DJ with 8 acid-tinged cuts that are equally expansive and inspiring, personal and inventive.

Sotofett spar and Tresor resident, Laura Sparrow aka LNS explores more atmospheric strains of her club sound, touching on Chicago deep house and Tin Man-esque acid, thru to flighty braindance jungle and electro

For 10 years LNS has built a staunch rep via countless sets at Treso’s Globus and dozens of drops for her LNS label and Sotofett’s Wania. She now takes the opportunity to spread wings on off-peak styles, following fine-wrought 303 lines into the chirruping shuffle of ‘Sweet Acid’, the Larry Heard-alike ‘Micro Acid’, and brisk Mike Dred-type flex of ‘Cosmacid’, to an electro-acid gem ‘Acid Rated’ comparable with classic Analords. It's still recognisably Mojave 3, but repackaged for the lucrative US market - hardly surprising then that the record's big tracks, 'Billoddity' and opener 'Bluebird of Happiness' were both synced to kingmaking TV show 'The O.C.'.
